## 1. What you'll build, and why

Phase 3 grows the *language*. We start with `struct` — Swift's fundamental building block and your
first **value type**. A struct bundles named **stored properties** into one aggregate, with a
**memberwise initializer** Swift gives you for free. Its defining behaviour is **value semantics**:
assigning a struct **copies** it, so changing the copy never affects the original. `Int`, `Bool`,
`Double`, `Array`, `String`, `Dictionary` — almost everything in Swift is a value type. This is the
single biggest design difference from most languages, and you're about to make it real.

- **You implement:** the value-type *lowering* — member **read** (`p.x`) and **write** (`p.x = e`)
  in SILGen, and the struct instructions in IRGen. The front end (parser, sema) is given.
- **Outcome:** struct programs **run and match swiftc**, value semantics included — the oracle
  test compiles a 16-program corpus with both compilers and compares every byte of output.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### A struct is an aggregate

`struct Point { var x: Int; var y: Int }` declares a type whose values are two `Int`s laid out
side by side — an **aggregate**. In LLVM that's a named type, `%Point = type { i64, i64 }`; a
`Point` variable is an `alloc_stack` slot big enough to hold both fields. Sema records each struct's
**layout** (its fields, in order) in a registry that SILGen and IRGen consult to turn a field *name*
into an *index*.

### Value semantics — the whole point

Watch what `var q = p` does:

![Value semantics: `var q = p` copies the whole aggregate into q's own slot, so `q.x = 99` changes only q — p still reads 1.](figs/value_semantics.png)

`q` gets its **own slot**, and the assignment **copies p's bytes into it**. From then on `p` and `q`
are completely independent: `q.x = 99` writes into q's slot and leaves p's slot alone. In our
memory-based SIL this falls out *for free* — `var q = p` lowers to `load` the whole aggregate out of
p's slot and `store` it into q's, and a field write goes through q's own address. There's no sharing
to begin with, so there's nothing to alias. (Contrast a **reference** type — a `class`, coming in a
later phase — where `q = p` copies a *pointer*, and both names see the same object. Value vs. reference
is *the* Swift distinction, and it's a property of how the type is copied, which is exactly what you
implement here.)

### Reading vs. writing a field — value vs. address

The two halves of member access are deliberately asymmetric, and the reason is lvalues:

- **Read `p.x`** wants a *value*. Lower `p` to a struct **value** (a `load`) and pull field `i` out
  with **`struct_extract`** (LLVM `extractvalue`). This works on *any* struct expression — a variable,
  a function result, a freshly built `Point(…)`.
- **Write `p.x = e`** must change `p` *in place*. You can't extract-modify-reinsert a copy; you need
  the **address** of the field inside p's slot. Take it with **`struct_element_addr`** (LLVM
  `getelementptr`) and `store` into it. This is only meaningful for an **lvalue** — a `var`-bound
  variable with a slot — which is exactly why `let`-bound structs reject field assignment, and why
  writing `q.x` can't possibly disturb `p`.

That read-uses-a-value / write-uses-an-address split is the lvalue/rvalue distinction every compiler
draws, made concrete.

### The memberwise initializer

`Point(x: 1, y: 2)` is the initializer Swift synthesizes from the stored properties — one labelled
argument per field, **in declaration order, labels required** (sema checks the labels and types; a
missing or wrong label is an error, just like swiftc). It lowers to a **`struct`** instruction that
builds the aggregate value from its fields (LLVM `insertvalue` from `undef`). Construction is given;
you build the access.

### The three new SIL instructions (swiftc's exact names)

| SIL | meaning | LLVM |
|---|---|---|
| `struct (%a, %b)` | build an aggregate from fields | `insertvalue` chain |
| `struct_extract %v, #i` | read field *i* from a struct **value** | `extractvalue` |
| `struct_element_addr %p, #i` | address of field *i* of a struct **address** | `getelementptr` |

swiftc emits these same instructions; the value/address split (`struct_extract` vs.
`struct_element_addr`) is straight from real SIL — read `swift/lib/SILGen/SILGenConstructor.cpp` for
the synthesized initializer and `swift/docs/SIL.rst` for the instructions.

### The subset you are growing into

**New lexemes.** Two punctuation marks and a keyword; the keyword table lives in `token.ml`
(`keyword_or_ident`), the punctuation in `lexer.ml`:

| spelling | token | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `struct` | `Token.Kw_struct` | a keyword, like `func` — it starts a top-level *item* |
| `.` | `Token.Dot` | shares the `'.'` arm with `..<`: peek for `.` `<` first, else it is a `Dot` |
| `;` | `Token.Newline` | Swift's statement separator; lexing it *as* a newline is what lets `struct P { var x: Int; var y: Int }` fit on one line |

No new operator, so the precedence table is concept 07's — member access is **postfix**, applied
after a primary is parsed and before any infix operator is considered, so it binds tighter than
everything.

**The grammar** — `<-- new` marks what this concept adds; everything else is concepts 05–09.
Notation is EBNF: `[ x ]` is *optional* (zero or one), `{ x }` is *repetition* (zero or more),
`|` separates alternatives, and quoted text is a terminal.

```
program     ::= { item NEWLINE }
item        ::= struct_decl                                        <-- new
              | func_decl
              | statement
struct_decl ::= "struct" ident "{" { field NEWLINE } "}"           <-- new
field       ::= ("var" | "let") ident ":" type                     <-- new

statement   ::= ("let" | "var") ident [ ":" type ] "=" expr
              | ident "=" expr
              | ident "." ident "=" expr                           <-- new (member write)
              | "if" expr block [ "else" ( block | if-statement ) ]
              | "while" expr block
              | "for" ident "in" expr "..<" expr block
              | "break" | "continue" | "return" [ expr ]
              | expr
block       ::= "{" { statement NEWLINE } "}"
type        ::= "Int" | "Double" | "Bool" | "String" | "Void"
              | ident                                              <-- new (a struct name)

expr        ::= or
or          ::= and { "||" and }                                     (bp 3)
and         ::= comparison { "&&" comparison }                       (bp 4)
comparison  ::= cast { ("==" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">=") cast } (bp 5)
cast        ::= sum { "as" type }                                    (bp 7)
sum         ::= product { ("+" | "-") product }                      (bp 10)
product     ::= unary { ("*" | "/" | "%") unary }                    (bp 20)
unary       ::= "-" unary | postfix
postfix     ::= primary { "." ident }                              <-- new (member read)
primary     ::= int | float | string | "true" | "false" | ident
              | ident "(" [ arg { "," arg } ] ")"
              | "(" expr ")"
arg         ::= [ ident ":" ] expr                                 <-- new (argument labels)
```

Three things to notice. A `struct` declaration is an **item**, not a statement — like `func`, it is
legal only at top level, so `parse_program` dispatches on `Kw_struct` and everything else still
goes to `parse_stmt`. The member *write* is a **statement production**, not an assignment to an
arbitrary expression: the parser commits to it on a four-token lookahead (`ident` `.` `ident` `=`),
which is why `l.b.x = 1` — two levels deep — is not in this subset. And a call argument may now
carry a **label**; the parser records it for every call, sema *checks* it only for a memberwise
initializer (a `func` still takes its arguments positionally, concept 07's simplification).

### The diagnostics sema owes you (given)

You write no diagnostics in this concept — sema is given — but the lowering may assume every rule
below has already fired, and `sema-structs.t` keeps them on record. Wording follows `swiftc
-typecheck` where the subset lets it (`swift/include/swift/AST/DiagnosticsSema.def`, line numbers
from the pinned snapshot); the differences are stated, not hidden.

| program | our message | swiftc |
|---|---|---|
| `Point(1, 2)` | `missing argument label 'x:' in call` (one per argument) | `missing argument labels 'x:y:' in call` — one message, plural (`missing_argument_labels`, l.1642) |
| `Point(z: 1, y: 2)` | `incorrect argument label in call (have 'z:', expected 'x:')` | `(have 'z:y:', expected 'x:y:')` — the whole label list (`wrong_argument_labels`, l.1646) |
| `Point(y: 2, x: 1)` | two `incorrect argument label` errors | `argument 'x' must precede argument 'y'` (`argument_out_of_order_named_named`, l.1651) |
| `Point(x: 1)` | `'Point' initializer expects 2 argument(s) but 1 given` | `missing argument for parameter 'y' in call` (`missing_argument_named`, l.1683) |
| `Point(x: "s", y: 2)` | `cannot convert value of type 'String' to specified type 'Int'` | `… to expected argument type 'Int'` (`cannot_convert_argument_value`, l.382) — we reuse 05's `check_expr` wording |
| `p.z`, `n.x` on an `Int` | `value of type 'Point' has no member 'z'` | **same** (`could_not_find_value_member`, l.70) |
| `let p …; p.x = 5` | `cannot assign to property: 'p' is a 'let' constant` | **same** (`assignment_lhs_is_immutable_property`, l.5379); swiftc points at the member, we at the statement |
| `struct S { let x: Int }; var s …; s.x = 2` | `cannot assign to property: 'x' is a 'let' constant` | **same** — a `let` field is immutable through every binding |
| `p == q` on structs | `binary operator '==' cannot be applied to two 'Point' operands` | **same** (`cannot_apply_binop_to_same_args`, l.220) — no `Equatable` until Exercise 3 |
| `let n: Int = p` | `cannot convert value of type 'Point' to specified type 'Int'` | **same** |
| `Nope(x: 1)` | `cannot find 'Nope' in scope` | **same** |
| `struct A {…}` twice | `invalid redeclaration of 'A'` | **same** (`invalid_redecl`, l.1110) |
| `print(p)` on a struct | `cannot print a value of type 'Point' (only Int, Double, Bool and String)` | **accepted** — swiftc prints `Point(x: 1, y: 2)` through reflection; ours has no runtime to do it, so sema refuses instead of letting IRGen crash |

Two more honest gaps of the v0 subset, both parser-level: a **nested write** `l.b.x = 1` is
not parsed (`Set_member` is one level, `p.x = e`; swiftc accepts it — Exercise 1's `mutating`
machinery is the natural place to generalize), and `print` of a `Double` goes through C's `%g`
(`3` where swiftc prints `3.0`), which is why the oracle corpus keeps to `Int`/`Bool` fields.

## 3. Build it, step by step

Front-end is done; fill the lowering.

- **`silgen.ml`** — two holes. In `gen_expr`, the `Member (e0, fld, _)` case is a **read**: lower
  `e0` to a struct *value*, ask its type (`vty`) which struct it is, and turn the field *name* into an
  *index* and a *type* through the layout in `b.structs` (`Types.field_index`, `Types.field_type`);
  the result is one `Sil.Struct_extract`. In `gen_stmt`, the `Set_member { obj; field; value }` case
  is a **write**: the variable's own slot is in `b.vars`, and its type names the struct; take the
  field's address with `Sil.Struct_element_addr` and `Sil.Store` the value through it. Generate the
  value first — that is the order swiftc uses, and the tests print the SIL.
- **`irgen.ml`** — one hole, three instructions: `Struct` is a chain of `insertvalue` starting
  from `undef` (each step names the previous register, the last one is the value); `Struct_extract`
  is `extractvalue`; `Struct_element_addr` is `getelementptr <struct ty>, ptr <slot>, i32 0, i32 i`.
  `llty (vty v)` gives the LLVM type of any value; `fresh ()` a register; `opnd` maps a SIL value to
  its LLVM operand.

Reference: `solution/` — after you have tried it.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase3-value-types/10-structs
```

Every `.t` file calls `./lab.exe`, built from **this directory's** library, so the report is about
your code here. In the order you fill the holes:

- `sema-structs.t` — `--typecheck`: the given rules from the table above, green from the start.
  It is the contract the lowering may rely on (no `p.x` on a non-struct reaches SILGen).
- `silgen-member-read.t` — `--emit-sil`: `p.x` is a `load` then `struct_extract … #0`; `p.y` is
  `#1` with its type; a field of a fresh `Point(…)` or of a call result extracts with no load; a
  nested `l.b.x` is two extracts; a read inside a function goes through the parameter's slot. No
  case writes a field, so this file goes green with the read hole alone.
- `silgen-member-write.t` — `--emit-sil`: `p.x = 9` is `struct_element_addr %slot, #0` and a
  `store`; the value is generated before the address; two writes share one slot; after `var q = p`
  the write addresses **q's** slot (value semantics, visible in the SIL); a write in a loop. No case
  reads a field.
- `irgen-structs.t` — `--emit-llvm` then `build`: the named type, the `insertvalue` chain (this
  first case needs no silgen hole), nested and mixed-type aggregates, `extractvalue`,
  `getelementptr`; then programs **run**: 3/4, the value-semantics `1`/`99`, by-value argument,
  struct result, field writes in a loop, and the `Double`-field case that pins a miscompile.
- `test_structs.ml` (alcotest `structs`) — the same four groups in-process: `sema-structs`
  (given — its four cases pass on the skeleton), `silgen-member-read`, `silgen-member-write`,
  `irgen-structs`.
- `oracle.t` — **the headline**, in two halves. The runtime half compiles the 16 programs of
  `oracle-corpus.txt` (value semantics, copies of nested structs, structs into and out of
  functions, field writes in loops, Bool fields) with `swiftc -Onone` and with `./lab.exe build`,
  runs both binaries, and demands identical stdout and exit code; when ours refuses with a
  `TODO(` the loop stops, so it stays red until the last hole is filled. The front-end half asks
  `swiftc -typecheck` and `./lab.exe --typecheck` for a verdict on the 20 programs of
  `typecheck-corpus.txt` — six well-formed, fourteen the struct rules must refuse — and they must
  agree; that half needs no lowering, so it is green from the start.

A hole you have not started shows as `TODO` with the list of what it will check; a hole in
progress shows `FAIL` with, under each failing case, what the test wants and what your code
printed. On the untouched skeleton the two silgen files and `irgen-structs.t` are `TODO`,
`sema-structs.t` is `PASS`, `oracle.t` is `FAIL` with its front-end half already `OK`, and the
alcotest is `FAIL` with its four sema cases `OK`.

## 5. Benchmark it

Value semantics has a cost: passing or assigning a big struct **copies every field**. Time a program
that copies a 6-field struct in a tight loop vs. swiftc. Swift's real answer for large aggregates is
**copy-on-write** (`Array`/`String` share storage until a mutation) — a Phase-7 optimization — and the
SIL optimizer (Phase 4) elides many copies outright. Our naive per-field copy is the honest baseline.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Methods + `mutating`.** Lower `struct Point { … func dist() -> Int { … } }` to a function with an
   implicit `self` parameter (read-only); a `mutating func` takes `self` by **address**
   (`struct_element_addr` territory) so it can write fields. This is how Swift threads `self`.
2. **Computed properties.** `var area: Int { return w * h }` — a property with a getter, lowered to a
   call, not a stored field. Distinguish stored vs. computed in the layout.
3. **`Equatable`.** Synthesize `==` for a struct (compare fields pairwise) — a first taste of Swift's
   protocol-conformance synthesis (full protocols are Phase 5, concept 21).

## 7. Recap & what's next

You added `struct` — a whole new **type kind** — through every stage, and made **value semantics**
real: structs are aggregates copied on assignment, with reads via `struct_extract` (a value) and
writes via `struct_element_addr` (an address into the variable's own slot). Programs run and match
swiftc.

Next, **11-enums-adts**: `enum` with associated values — **tagged unions**, the other half of
algebraic data types. Where a struct is "all of these fields at once" (a product), an enum is "exactly
one of these cases" (a sum), laid out as a **tag + payload**. Then **12-pattern-matching** gives you
`switch` to take them apart — and **13-optionals** reveals that `Optional` was just an enum all along.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

From `solution/silgen.ml` (the access) and `solution/irgen.ml` (the LLVM):

```ocaml
(* SILGen — member read is a value; member write is an address *)
| Ast.Member (e0, fld, _) ->
    let sv = gen_expr b e0 in
    let sn = match vty b sv with Types.TStruct sn -> sn | _ -> assert false in
    let sl = Hashtbl.find b.structs sn in
    emit b (Sil.Struct_extract (sv, Option.get (Types.field_index sl fld)))
      (Option.get (Types.field_type sl fld))

| Ast.Set_member { obj; field; value; _ } ->
    let v = gen_expr b value in
    let slot = Hashtbl.find b.vars obj in                 (* p's OWN slot — value semantics *)
    let sn = match vty b slot with Types.TStruct sn -> sn | _ -> assert false in
    let sl = Hashtbl.find b.structs sn in
    let faddr = emit b (Sil.Struct_element_addr (slot, Option.get (Types.field_index sl field)))
                  (Option.get (Types.field_type sl field)) in
    ignore (emit b (Sil.Store (v, faddr)) Types.TVoid)
```

```ocaml
(* IRGen — aggregates in LLVM *)
| Sil.Struct fields ->
    let sty = llty (vty v) in
    let acc = ref "undef" in
    List.iteri (fun idx fv ->
      let r = fresh () in
      p (Printf.sprintf "  %s = insertvalue %s %s, %s %s, %d\n" r sty !acc (llty (vty fv)) (op fv) idx);
      acc := r) fields;
    Hashtbl.replace opnd v !acc
| Sil.Struct_extract (a, idx) ->
    let r = fresh () in
    p (Printf.sprintf "  %s = extractvalue %s %s, %d\n" r (llty (vty a)) (op a) idx);
    Hashtbl.replace opnd v r
| Sil.Struct_element_addr (a, idx) ->
    let r = fresh () in
    p (Printf.sprintf "  %s = getelementptr %s, ptr %s, i32 0, i32 %d\n" r (llty (vty a)) (op a) idx);
    Hashtbl.replace opnd v r
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — methods and `mutating`

Parse a `func` inside a `struct` body; lower it to a SIL function named e.g. `Point.dist` with an
extra first parameter `self`. A **non-mutating** method takes `self` by value (a copy — reads only); a
**`mutating`** method takes `self` by **address** (a pointer to the caller's slot) so its
`self.x = …` writes back via `struct_element_addr`. A call `p.dist()` passes `p` (by value) or `&p`
(its address, for mutating) as the first argument. This is exactly how Swift desugars methods.

### 2 — computed properties

Add a `computed` flag (or a separate list) to the layout: a computed property has a getter body, not a
slot. Member access on a computed property lowers to a **call** to the getter, not a `struct_extract`.
Stored and computed properties read the same at the call site (`p.area`), which is the point — uniform
access.

### 3 — `Equatable`

When a struct is used with `==`, synthesize a function that returns the `&&` of `a.fᵢ == b.fᵢ` over all
fields. Register it so `infer_binary`'s `Eq` case accepts two `TStruct sn` operands. This is the
gentlest case of Swift's *derived conformances*; the general mechanism (protocols + witness tables) is
Phase 5 (concept 21).
```
